name: Animalia
description: Multicellular, eukaryotic organisms that are heterotrophic, typically motile, and develop from a blastula.
keyCharacteristics: Mostly motile at some life stage
diagnosticFeatures: Multicellular eukaryotes that ingest other organisms (heterotrophic nutrition)
Cells without rigid walls; collagen and structural proteins common
Active movement at some life stage in most groups
Sexual reproduction typical, with a motile sperm and larger egg
Embryonic development usually passing through a blastula stage

name: Chordata
description: Animals possessing a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and post-anal tail at some developmental stage.

name: Porifera
description: Porifera are the simplest multicellular animals — sessile, mostly marine filter-feeders whose porous bodies pump water through a canal system to trap food and oxygen.
keyCharacteristics: Porous body with inhalant pores (ostia) and a single exhalant opening (osculum)
Water-canal system driven by collar cells (choanocytes)
Skeleton of calcareous or siliceous spicules, spongin fibres, or both
diagnosticFeatures: Cellular level of organisation — no true tissues or organs
Acoelomate; no digestive, circulatory or nervous system

name: Cnidaria
description: Cnidaria are aquatic, mostly marine animals with radial symmetry and tissue-level organisation, armed with stinging cnidocytes — jellyfish, corals, sea anemones and hydroids.
keyCharacteristics: Stinging cells (cnidocytes) bearing nematocysts for defence and prey capture
Two body forms: sessile polyp and free-swimming medusa
Blind gastrovascular cavity with a single opening
Nerve net without a centralised brain
Mostly marine; a few freshwater forms such as Hydra

name: Ctenophora
description: Ctenophora, the comb jellies, are exclusively marine, free-swimming predators that row through the water with eight bands of ciliated comb plates.
keyCharacteristics: Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates (ctenes) for locomotion
Sticky prey-capturing cells (colloblasts) instead of stinging cells
diagnosticFeatures: Complete gut with anal pores (unlike cnidarians)

name: Platyhelminthes
description: Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, are soft, dorsoventrally flattened worms — the simplest bilaterally symmetrical triploblastic animals, including free-living planarians and parasitic flukes and tapeworms.
keyCharacteristics: Free-living planarians as well as endoparasitic flukes and tapeworms
Excretion and osmoregulation by flame cells (protonephridia)
Mostly hermaphrodite; remarkable regeneration in free-living forms
diagnosticFeatures: Organ level of organisation; gut incomplete or absent

name: Nematoda
description: Nematoda, the roundworms, are cylindrical, unsegmented pseudocoelomate worms found in soil, water and as parasites of plants and animals — among the most numerous animals on Earth.
keyCharacteristics: Slender cylindrical body, circular in cross-section, covered by a tough cuticle
Complete digestive tract with mouth and anus
Free-living soil and aquatic forms plus many plant and animal parasites
Separate sexes, usually with visible sexual dimorphism

name: Annelida
description: Annelida, the segmented worms, are coelomate worms with metamerically segmented bodies — earthworms, leeches and marine ragworms — with closed circulation and excretion by nephridia.
keyCharacteristics: Metamerically segmented body with repeating internal organs
Closed circulatory system, often with haemoglobin-like pigment
Locomotion aided by chaetae (setae); leeches bear suckers

name: Arthropoda
description: Arthropoda, the jointed-legged animals, is the largest animal phylum — insects, spiders, crabs and centipedes — protected by a moulted chitinous exoskeleton and moving on jointed appendages.
keyCharacteristics: Segmented body with paired jointed appendages
Chitinous exoskeleton, periodically shed by moulting (ecdysis)
Open circulatory system with haemocoel body cavity
Respiration by gills, tracheae or book lungs according to group
Roughly two-thirds of all described animal species

name: Mollusca
description: Mollusca, the soft-bodied animals, is the second-largest phylum — snails, clams, squids and octopuses — built on a head-foot, visceral mass and mantle that usually secretes a calcareous shell.
keyCharacteristics: Body of head-foot, visceral mass and dorsal mantle
Mantle usually secretes a calcareous shell (reduced or absent in squids and octopuses)
Rasping feeding organ, the radula (absent in bivalves)

name: Echinodermata
description: Echinodermata, the spiny-skinned animals, are exclusively marine coelomates — starfish, sea urchins, brittle stars and sea cucumbers — moving on a unique water vascular system with tube feet.
keyCharacteristics: Five-rayed (pentamerous) radial symmetry in adults; bilateral larvae
Water vascular system with tube feet for locomotion and feeding
Calcareous endoskeleton of ossicles, often with surface spines
Exclusively marine; remarkable powers of regeneration

name: Hemichordata
description: Hemichordata, the acorn worms, are marine worm-like animals with a three-part body (proboscis, collar, trunk), pharyngeal gill slits and a stomochord — a living link between non-chordates and chordates.
keyCharacteristics: Three body regions: proboscis, collar and trunk
Pharyngeal gill slits for filter feeding
Stomochord (buccal diverticulum) in the collar region
Marine burrowers; tornaria larvae resembling echinoderm larvae

name: Mammalia
description: Vertebrates characterized by mammary glands, hair/fur, three middle ear bones, and neocortex.
keyCharacteristics: Hair or fur at some stage
Three middle ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes)
diagnosticFeatures: Viviparous (mostly) with placental or marsupial reproduction

name: Carnivora
description: Placental mammals specialized for meat-eating, with carnassial teeth for shearing flesh.
diagnosticFeatures: Dental formula typically I 3/3, C 1/1, P 4/4, M 2/3 = 42 (reduced in some)

name: Proboscidea
description: Large herbivorous mammals characterized by a trunk (proboscis), tusks, and massive pillar-like limbs.
keyCharacteristics: Trunk (fusion of nose and upper lip)
diagnosticFeatures: Dental replacement: 6 sets of molars sequentially

name: Felidae
description: Cats — obligate carnivores with retractable claws, specialized teeth, and muscular bodies.

name: Canidae
description: Dogs, wolves, foxes, jackals — cursorial carnivores with non-retractable claws and complex social behavior.

name: Elephantidae
description: Elephants and extinct relatives (mammoths, mastodons) — the only living proboscidean family.
diagnosticFeatures: Dental battery: 6 sequential molars per quadrant

name: Elephas
description: Asian elephants — the only living genus of the family Elephantidae, containing the Asian elephant and extinct relatives.
diagnosticFeatures: Distinct from Loxodonta (African elephants) by ear size, back shape, trunk fingers
Extinct species include E. antiquus, E. namadicus

name: Panthera
description: Roaring cats — tiger, lion, leopard, jaguar, snow leopard. Characterized by incompletely ossified hyoid enabling roar.

name: Vulpes
description: True foxes — small to medium canids with pointed muzzles, large ears, and bushy tails.

name: Panthera tigris
description: Tiger — largest living cat, striped coat, apex predator across Asia.

name: Elephas maximus
description: Asian elephant — largest land animal in Asia, single trunk finger, convex back.

name: Vulpes vulpes
description: Red fox — most widely distributed carnivore, highly adaptable, omnivorous.
keyCharacteristics: Reddish coat with white tail tip
Black ear tips and leg stockings

name: Panthera tigris tigris
description: Bengal tiger — nominate subspecies, Indian subcontinent, mangrove-adapted (Sundarbans).
keyCharacteristics: Orange coat with narrow black stripes
National animal of India and Bangladesh
diagnosticFeatures: Darker and smaller than P. t. altaica

name: Actinopterygii
description: Actinopterygii, the ray-finned fishes, are bony fishes whose fins are supported by bony rays — the largest vertebrate class, from carps and catfish relatives to perches, including most familiar freshwater and marine food fishes.
keyCharacteristics: Fins supported by flexible bony rays (lepidotrichia)
Bony skeleton with ganoid, cycloid or ctenoid scales
Gas-filled swim bladder for buoyancy control
External fertilisation typical; enormous diversity of body forms
diagnosticFeatures: Single dorsal nerve cord with lateral-line sensory system

name: Cypriniformes
description: Cypriniformes — carps, minnows, loaches and suckers — is the largest order of freshwater fishes, toothless-jawed bottom and column feeders with a Weberian apparatus linking the swim bladder to hearing.
keyCharacteristics: Jaws without teeth; food ground by throat (pharyngeal) teeth
Weberian apparatus connecting swim bladder to the inner ear
Smooth cycloid scales; single soft-rayed dorsal fin (mostly)
Dominant fishes of Asian and European fresh waters, including major food carps

name: Clupeiformes
description: Clupeiformes — herrings, shads, sardines and anchovies, including the hilsa — are silvery schooling fishes feeding on plankton, prized worldwide as food fishes with several major migratory species.
keyCharacteristics: Deep silvery compressed body built for schooling
Single short dorsal fin; forked tail for sustained swimming
Includes famous migratory food fishes such as the hilsa
diagnosticFeatures: Abdominal scutes (keeled belly scales) in many species
Physostomous swim bladder connected to the gut

name: Elasmobranchii
description: Elasmobranchii — sharks, rays, skates and sawfish — are fishes with cartilaginous skeletons, exposed gill slits and placoid scales, including the largest living fish, the whale shark.
keyCharacteristics: Skeleton of cartilage rather than bone
Five to seven exposed gill slits on each side; no gill cover
Skin armoured with tooth-like placoid denticles
No swim bladder; large oily liver aids buoyancy
Slow growth and low fecundity; vulnerable to overfishing
diagnosticFeatures: Internal fertilisation with claspers in males

name: Orectolobiformes
description: Orectolobiformes, the carpet sharks, are bottom-associated sharks with sensory barbels and small mouths — an order that also contains the whale shark, the largest living fish.
keyCharacteristics: Short sensory barbels on the snout
Small transverse mouth positioned ahead of the eyes
Two spineless dorsal fins set far back on the body
Mostly bottom-dwelling; includes the filter-feeding whale shark
diagnosticFeatures: Nostrils connected to the mouth by grooves
Fifth gill slit overlapping the fourth

name: Myliobatiformes
description: Myliobatiformes — stingrays, eagle rays and manta rays — are flattened cartilaginous fishes that swim by flapping enlarged pectoral fins, including the giant filter-feeding manta rays.
keyCharacteristics: Disc-shaped flattened body with wing-like pectoral fins
Whip-like tail, venomous spine in most stingrays (absent in mantas)
Crushing tooth plates suited to shellfish prey
diagnosticFeatures: Gill slits entirely on the underside
Spiracles behind the eyes for breathing while buried
Enlarged brain and complex behaviour in mantas

name: Siluriformes
description: Siluriformes, the catfishes, are scaleless fishes recognised by sensory barbels around the mouth — a huge freshwater order including large river predators and important food fishes.
keyCharacteristics: Prominent sensory barbels (whiskers) around the mouth
Scaleless skin, often with bony head plates
Strong locking pectoral and dorsal spines for defence
Weberian hearing apparatus; many tolerate low-oxygen waters
diagnosticFeatures: Adipose fin present in many families

name: Anabantiformes
description: Anabantiformes — climbing perches, snakeheads and gouramis — are freshwater fishes of Asia and Africa equipped with a labyrinth organ that lets them breathe air and survive oxygen-poor waters.
keyCharacteristics: Labyrinth organ above the gills for breathing atmospheric air
Hardy in warm, shallow, oxygen-poor fresh waters
Includes air-gulping snakeheads and nest-building gouramis
Several important food and aquarium fishes

name: Gobiiformes
description: Gobiiformes, the gobies and sleepers, are mostly small bottom-dwelling fishes whose fused pelvic fins form a sucking disc for clinging to substrates in marine, fresh and brackish waters.
keyCharacteristics: Pelvic fins fused into a ventral sucking disc
Huge species number across marine and freshwater habitats
diagnosticFeatures: Fin-spine and soft-ray dorsal fins usually separate

name: Malacostraca
description: Malacostraca is the largest crustacean class — crabs, shrimps, lobsters, krill and woodlice — with a segmented body, jointed biramous limbs and usually a protective carapace over the head and thorax.
keyCharacteristics: Body of head, thorax and abdomen (typically 19–20 segments)
Carapace covering head and thorax in most groups
Jointed, often biramous appendages specialised per segment
Includes the most valuable marine food crustaceans
diagnosticFeatures: Open circulatory system with dorsal heart
Respiration by gills; excretion by antennal glands

name: Decapoda
description: Decapoda — crabs, shrimps, prawns and lobsters — are ten-legged crustaceans whose front legs often bear claws, with a cephalothorax armoured by a carapace; the most economically important shellfish group.
keyCharacteristics: Five pairs of walking legs; first pair often clawed (chelate)
Well-developed abdomen ending in a tail fan for swimming flips
Includes prawns, crabs, lobsters and hermit crabs
diagnosticFeatures: Complex larval series (nauplius to adult stages)

name: Reptilia
description: Reptilia — turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodilians and the tuatara — are ectothermic amniotes with dry, scaly skin and shelled eggs that freed vertebrates from breeding in water.
keyCharacteristics: Dry skin with keratin scales or scutes limiting water loss
Amniotic eggs with protective shells (mostly egg-laying)
Ectothermic regulation of body temperature by behaviour
diagnosticFeatures: Single occipital condyle at the skull base

name: Testudines
description: Testudines — turtles, tortoises and terrapins — are the oldest living reptile order, armoured in a bony shell of carapace and plastron, toothless-beaked and egg-laying on land or beaches.
keyCharacteristics: Bony shell of dorsal carapace and ventral plastron
Horny toothless beak instead of teeth
Limbs modified as flippers, feet or elephantine legs by habitat
Long-lived; many marine species migrate to nesting beaches
diagnosticFeatures: Ribs and vertebrae fused into the shell
Oviparous with temperature-influenced development in many species

name: Cephalopoda
description: Cephalopoda — octopuses, squids, cuttlefish and nautiluses — are active marine molluscs with closed circulation, advanced eyes and brains, sucker-bearing arms and rapid jet propulsion.
keyCharacteristics: Arms and tentacles with suckers surrounding the mouth
Closed circulatory system — unique among molluscs
Large image-forming eyes and the most advanced invertebrate brain
Jet propulsion by mantle contractions; ink sac for defence (except nautiluses)
diagnosticFeatures: Shell external only in nautiluses; internal or absent otherwise
Direct development without a true larval stage
Bilateral symmetry with dorsoventrally specialised body axis

name: Octopoda
description: Octopoda, the octopuses, are eight-armed cephalopods without internal shells — soft-bodied, highly intelligent molluscs famed for camouflage, escape artistry and problem-solving.
keyCharacteristics: Eight sucker-bearing arms and no feeding tentacles
Completely soft body with no internal shell
Rapid colour and texture camouflage via chromatophores
Short lives with a single terminal breeding episode
diagnosticFeatures: Arms joined at the base by a web
Ink sac present; internal shell absent

name: Cetacea
description: Cetacea — whales, dolphins and porpoises — are fully aquatic mammals that breathe air through a blowhole, nurse their young with milk and navigate by hearing, including echolocation in toothed whales.
keyCharacteristics: Forelimbs modified into flippers; hind limbs lost; horizontal tail flukes
Breathing through a dorsal blowhole; thick blubber insulation
Baleen plates in filter-feeding whales, teeth in hunters
Complex social lives and long migrations in many species
diagnosticFeatures: Mammalian endothermy, live birth and lactation in water
Nostrils migrated to the top of the skull

description: Monkeys, apes, lorises and kin: forward-facing eyes, grasping hands and large brains.
keyCharacteristics: Grasping hands and feet with nails
Large brain relative to body size
diagnosticFeatures: Single pair of mammary glands on chest

name: Chiroptera
description: Bats: the only mammals capable of powered flight.
keyCharacteristics: Many use echolocation for night navigation
Hind limbs rotated for roosting head-down
diagnosticFeatures: Single offspring typical in many species

name: Hylobatidae
description: Gibbons: small tailless apes of Asian canopies.

name: Mustelidae
description: Weasels, otters and kin: elongated carnivorans, many semi-aquatic.

name: Cercopithecidae
description: Old World monkeys: macaques and kin with cheek pouches.

name: Pteropodidae

name: Macaca

description: Short-nosed fruit bats of orchards and forest edge.

name: Nycticebus

name: Crocodilia

diagnosticFeatures: Secondary palate for breathing while submerged

name: Pythonidae

name: Colubridae

keyCharacteristics: Strong swimming limbs or elephantine legs

name: Gavialidae

name: Python
description: True pythons of Africa and Asia.

name: Bungarus
description: Kraits: banded nocturnal elapids.
diagnosticFeatures: Small head barely distinct from neck

name: Naja
description: True cobras with hooding display.

name: Ophiophagus
description: King cobra: the snake-eating giant.

name: Pangshura
description: Roofed turtles of South Asian rivers.

name: Geoclemys
description: Spotted pond turtles.

name: Gavialis
description: Gharials.

name: Amphibia
description: Amphibians: vertebrates living part of life in water and part on land.
diagnosticFeatures: Eggs without shells laid in water

name: Anura
description: Frogs and toads: tailless jumping amphibians.

name: Bufonidae
description: True toads: warty, parotoid-glanded amphibians.

name: Dicroglossidae
description: Fork-tongued frogs of Asian wetlands and paddies.

name: Microhylidae

name: Rhacophoridae

description: Skittering and pond frogs.

name: Microhyla
description: Narrow-mouthed frogs.

name: Polypedates
description: Whippping and tree frogs of Asia.

keyCharacteristics: Three body regions with six legs

name: Lepidoptera
description: Butterflies and moths: scaled-wing insects.

name: Papilionidae
description: Swallowtails: large butterflies, many tailed.

name: Nymphalidae
description: Brush-footed butterflies: the largest family.

name: Pieridae
description: Whites and yellows: pierid butterflies.

description: Palaemonid shrimps and prawns.

description: Swallowtails including mormons and limes.

description: Jezebels: mistletoe-feeding pierids.

description: Blue tigers: migratory danaid butterflies.

name: Euploea
description: Crows: dark unpalatable danaid butterflies.

name: Macrobrachium
description: Freshwater prawns including the giant river prawn.

name: Chromadorea
description: Chromadorea is the larger nematode class — mostly terrestrial and freshwater roundworms with pocket-like sense organs (amphids), including free-living models such as Caenorhabditis and major parasites such as Ascaris.
keyCharacteristics: Amphid sense organs typically pocket- or spiral-shaped
Excretory system usually with lateral canals
Mostly terrestrial and freshwater; free-living and parasitic forms
Includes Rhabditida (model organisms) and Ascaridida (large animal parasites)
diagnosticFeatures: Males often with copulatory bursa in parasitic groups

name: Enoplea
description: Enoplea are mostly marine and soil nematodes with simple pocket-less sense organs — an ancient lineage including free-living marine Enoplida and the muscle-dwelling Trichinella relatives.
keyCharacteristics: Simple excretory cell rather than canal systems (mostly)
Includes Enoplida and other early-branching orders
diagnosticFeatures: Cuticle often smooth with fine striations
Stichosome oesophagus in several parasitic groups

name: Rhabditida
description: Rhabditida are small free-living and parasitic nematodes with a double-bulbed feeding tube — the order of the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans and many soil and insect-associated species.
keyCharacteristics: Double posterior bulb (grinder) in the oesophagus
Small free-living soil forms plus insect and vertebrate associates
Includes Caenorhabditis, a cornerstone of genetic research
Rapid life cycles suited to ephemeral habitats
diagnosticFeatures: Rhabditoid oesophagus with median and terminal bulbs

name: Ascaridida
description: Ascaridida are large intestinal roundworms of vertebrates — Ascaris, dog and cat roundworms — with three prominent lips and complex migratory life cycles through host tissues.
keyCharacteristics: Three characteristic lips around the mouth opening
Eggs with thick protective shells surviving in soil
Larval migration through liver and lungs in many species
diagnosticFeatures: Excretory nucleus in the oesophageal region

name: Enoplida
description: Enoplida are mostly free-living marine nematodes with a spacious barrel-shaped feeding cavity — abundant predators and omnivores of seabed sediments worldwide.
keyCharacteristics: Dominant free-living nematodes of marine sediments
Slender bodies with visible internal organisation
Important links in benthic food webs

name: Turbellaria
description: Turbellaria are mostly free-living flatworms — planarians gliding on ciliated undersides through freshwater, marine and damp terrestrial habitats, famous for regeneration.
keyCharacteristics: Extraordinary regeneration from tiny body fragments
diagnosticFeatures: Branched intestine distributing food without a circulatory system

name: Trematoda
description: Trematoda, the flukes, are parasitic flatworms with muscular suckers that cling inside vertebrate organs — liver flukes and blood flukes with complex multi-host life cycles.
keyCharacteristics: Muscular oral and ventral suckers for attachment
Complex life cycles alternating sexual and asexual generations
Freshwater snails almost always serve as first hosts
Includes agents of fascioliasis and schistosomiasis

name: Cestoda
description: Cestoda, the tapeworms, are long ribbon-like intestinal parasites built of repeating segments — head (scolex) with hooks and suckers, neck, and a chain of egg-filled proglottids, with no gut of their own.
keyCharacteristics: Scolex with suckers, hooks or grooves anchoring the worm
Body of repeating segments (proglottids) budded from a neck region
No digestive tract; nutrients absorbed through the skin
Eggs released in mature segments via intermediate hosts
diagnosticFeatures: Lack of mouth and gut at all stages

name: Tricladida
description: Tricladida are three-branched-gut planarians — the familiar freshwater flatworms of ponds and streams, model animals for regeneration and stem-cell biology.
keyCharacteristics: Three-branched intestine (one forward, two rear branches)
diagnosticFeatures: Pharynx opening mid-body on the underside

name: Plagiorchiida
description: Plagiorchiida is the largest fluke order — liver, lung and intestinal flukes of vertebrates, including Fasciola, cycling through snails to livestock, wildlife and people.
keyCharacteristics: Two-sucker body plan with spined skin in many species
Snail first hosts; vertebrate definitive hosts
Includes liver flukes of major veterinary importance
diagnosticFeatures: Laurer’s canal present in most families

name: Cyclophyllidea
description: Cyclophyllidea are the familiar tapeworms of people, livestock and pets — Taenia and relatives — cycling between intermediate hosts and carnivore intestines.
keyCharacteristics: Four muscular suckers on a compact scolex, often with hooks
Mammals and birds as definitive hosts
Includes beef, pork and dwarf tapeworms of medical importance
diagnosticFeatures: Vitelline gland single and compact behind the ovary
Genital pores alternating irregularly along the segments

name: Trichinellida
description: Trichinellida are tissue-dwelling nematodes of vertebrates — the order of Trichinella, whose larvae encyst in host muscle and complete the cycle when eaten.
keyCharacteristics: Parasites of vertebrate muscle and gut tissues
Larvae encysted in host muscle as the infective stage
Transmission by carnivory of infected flesh
Stichosome oesophagus of stacked gland cells
diagnosticFeatures: No intermediate host required for the basic cycle

name: Ascarididae
description: Ascarididae are large intestinal roundworms of vertebrates — Ascaris of people and pigs — with three lips and migratory larvae; current treatments place the family within Rhabditida.
keyCharacteristics: Three prominent lips around the mouth
Thick-shelled eggs surviving months in soil
Larval migration through host liver and lungs
diagnosticFeatures: Triradiate oesophagus without a posterior bulb
Males with paired spicules and no bursa

name: Oxyuridae
description: Oxyuridae, the pinworms, are small intestinal nematodes with a double-bulbed oesophagus — Enterobius of humans and relatives of rodents, primates and other mammals.
keyCharacteristics: Small worms with a double posterior oesophageal bulb
Females migrate to lay eggs around the host’s outlet
Direct life cycle without intermediate hosts
Commonest intestinal worm infection of people worldwide
diagnosticFeatures: Cephalic inflations at the head end

name: Rhabditidae
description: Rhabditidae are small free-living soil nematodes with a double-bulbed oesophagus — the family of the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans.
keyCharacteristics: Free-living bacterial feeders of soil and compost
Short rapid life cycles; many self-fertilising hermaphrodites

name: Ancylostomatidae
description: Ancylostomatidae, the hookworms, are blood-feeding intestinal nematodes whose larvae enter hosts through skin — major agents of anaemia in people and livestock.
keyCharacteristics: Cutting plates or teeth gripping the intestinal wall
Larvae penetrating skin from contaminated soil
diagnosticFeatures: Buccal capsule armed with teeth or plates
Single direct life cycle with free-living larval stages

name: Trichinellidae
description: Trichinellidae contains Trichinella — thread-like muscle parasites cycling between carnivores when infected flesh is eaten; cause of trichinellosis in people.
keyCharacteristics: Hair-thin adults embedded in host intestine
Newborn larvae carried by blood to striped muscle
Larvae coiling and encysting inside muscle cells
No egg stage outside the host
diagnosticFeatures: Stichosome oesophagus along the front body

name: Ascaris
description: Ascaris are giant intestinal roundworms of people and pigs — among the largest nematode parasites of humans, with thick-shelled eggs and tissue-migrating larvae.
keyCharacteristics: Very large pale worms (females to about 35 cm)
Three-lipped mouth for anchoring to gut contents
diagnosticFeatures: Vulva positioned toward the front third

name: Enterobius
description: Enterobius are human pinworms — small white worms of the large intestine whose egg-laying migrations cause the familiar childhood infection.
keyCharacteristics: Small white worms visible around the outlet at night
Human-specific life cycle with hand-to-mouth spread
Diagnosed by egg recovery from the surrounding skin

name: Caenorhabditis
description: Caenorhabditis are tiny free-living soil nematodes — the genus of C. elegans, the first animal with a fully mapped cell lineage and nervous system.
keyCharacteristics: Millimetre-long transparent bodies ideal for microscopy
Three-day generation time on bacterial lawns
Entire genome and neural wiring charted
diagnosticFeatures: Fixed number of body cells in adults

name: Ancylostoma
description: Ancylostoma are Old World hookworms — blood-feeding gut parasites entering through skin, a leading cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in tropical regions.
keyCharacteristics: Hooked head end gripping the intestinal lining
Chronic blood loss and protein deficiency in heavy infections
Dogs, cats and people host closely related species

name: Trichinella
description: Trichinella are muscle-encysting nematodes cycling between carnivores — the agent of trichinellosis acquired from raw or undercooked pork and game.
keyCharacteristics: Adults embedded in the small-intestinal lining
Larvae encysted in striped muscle as the durable stage
Cycle completed by eating infected flesh
Controlled by meat inspection and thorough cooking

name: Taeniidae
description: Taeniidae are tapeworms of carnivores — Taenia and Echinococcus — cycling through herbivore and omnivore intermediate hosts, including major zoonoses of people.
keyCharacteristics: Compact scolex with four suckers, often with hooks
Larval cysts (cysticerci, hydatids) in intermediate hosts
Includes pork tapeworm and hydatid agents
diagnosticFeatures: Unarmed or armed scolex with acetabula
Genital pores alternating along the segments

name: Fasciolidae
description: Fasciolidae are large leaf-shaped flukes of livestock livers — Fasciola species cycling through amphibious snails to grazing animals and people.
keyCharacteristics: Broad leaf-like body with branched gut and gonads
Snail intermediate hosts in wet pastures
Infective cysts clinging to water plants
diagnosticFeatures: Branched testes and ovary filling the body

name: Opisthorchiidae
description: Opisthorchiidae are small fish-borne liver flukes — Clonorchis and relatives cycling through snails and freshwater fish to fish-eating mammals.
keyCharacteristics: Small flattened flukes of bile ducts and gall bladder
Two-host cycle: snails, then freshwater fish
Human infection from raw or undercooked fish
Chronic infection linked to bile-duct disease
diagnosticFeatures: Excretory bladder S-shaped behind forked gut
Genital pore ahead of the ventral sucker

name: Dugesiidae
description: Dugesiidae are freshwater triclad planarians — the family of the regeneration model Schmidtea — with arrow heads, eyespots and a three-branched gut.
keyCharacteristics: Three-branched intestine visible through the body
Gliding hunters of small freshwater prey

name: Taenia
description: Taenia are large tapeworms of carnivore intestines — pork and beef tapeworms of people — with hooked or unhooked scolices and egg-filled terminal segments.
keyCharacteristics: Metre-long chains of segments in the definitive host gut
Infective cysticerci in muscle and organs
Among the longest parasites of humans
diagnosticFeatures: Four suckers; hooks present or absent by species
Gravid segments packed with branched uteri

name: Echinococcus
description: Echinococcus are tiny dog tapeworms whose hydatid cysts grow in livestock and people — agents of cystic echinococcosis, a major global zoonosis.
keyCharacteristics: Minute adults of only a few segments in dog intestines
Slow-growing fluid-filled hydatid cysts in intermediate hosts
Dogs and livestock completing the cycle near people
Preventable by dog deworming and offal control
diagnosticFeatures: Scolex with hooks in two rows
Sac-like uterus in the single gravid segment

name: Fasciola
description: Fasciola are large liver flukes of grazing animals and people — leaf-shaped worms of bile ducts reached by eating water plants carrying cysts.
keyCharacteristics: Broad leaf-like body with a conical front projection
Snail hosts in ditches and wet grazing
Infection from watercress and other aquatic plants
Major cause of livestock liver condemnation
diagnosticFeatures: Highly branched gut and reproductive organs
Shoulder-like widening behind the head cone

name: Clonorchis
description: Clonorchis are small liver flukes of East Asia reaching people through raw freshwater fish — long-lived bile-duct parasites of fish-eating mammals.
keyCharacteristics: Small flattened flukes resident in bile ducts
Decades-long infections from repeated raw-fish meals
Controlled by cooking fish and sanitation
diagnosticFeatures: Branched testes in tandem at the rear body
Dark egg-filled uterus filling the mid-body

name: Schmidtea
description: Schmidtea are freshwater triclad planarians — the genus of S. mediterranea, a stem-cell and regeneration model with a sequenced genome and asexual strains.
keyCharacteristics: Small arrow-headed hunters of ponds and streams
Famous asexual strains regenerating entire bodies
Central model for stem cells and tissue patterning

name: Calcarea
description: Calcarea are calcareous sponges whose spicules are made of calcium carbonate — small, often tubular or vase-shaped sponges of shallow waters, including Sycon.
keyCharacteristics: Often small tubular, vase or branching growth forms
diagnosticFeatures: Choanocytes relatively large with central nuclei

name: Hexactinellida
description: Hexactinellida, the glass sponges, build six-rayed siliceous skeletons — deep-water vase and lattice sponges such as the Venus’ flower basket.
keyCharacteristics: Skeleton of six-rayed (hexactine) siliceous spicules, often fused
Mostly deep-water vase, cup or lattice forms
Syncytial tissue organisation unique among sponges
diagnosticFeatures: Glass-like fused skeleton in many species

name: Homoscleromorpha
description: Homoscleromorpha are mostly encrusting marine sponges with a distinct basement membrane — a small class confirmed by Catalogue of Life as a separate poriferan lineage.
keyCharacteristics: Thin encrusting or cushion growth on hard substrates
True basement membrane beneath the outer cell layer

name: Spongillida
description: Spongillida are freshwater demosponges — green encrusting sponges of lakes and rivers that survive winter as resistant gemmules.
keyCharacteristics: Green colour from symbiotic algae in many species
Dormant gemmules surviving drying and freezing

name: Dictyoceratida
description: Dictyoceratida are horny sponges whose skeleton is spongin fibre alone — the bath sponges harvested since antiquity.
keyCharacteristics: Skeleton of spongin fibres without mineral spicules

name: Clionaida
description: Clionaida are boring sponges that chemically excavate limestone, shells and coral — major bioeroders of reefs alongside free-living forms.

name: Leucosolenida
description: Leucosolenida are tubular calcareous sponges — delicate white clusters such as Sycon common on shaded marine rocks and shells.

name: Clathrinida
description: Clathrinida are small cushion-like calcareous sponges — yellow network sponges such as Clathrina coating shaded rocks.
keyCharacteristics: Cushion or network growth of fused tubes
diagnosticFeatures: Calcareous triactines without a differentiated skeleton

name: Lyssacinosida
description: Lyssacinosida are loose-spiculed glass sponges — including the Venus’ flower basket and giant cloud sponges of deep reefs.
keyCharacteristics: Vase, funnel or branching deep-water forms

name: Haplosclerida
description: Haplosclerida are soft demosponges with simple skeletons — branching and tubular forms such as Haliclona common on reefs and pilings.
keyCharacteristics: Soft compressible texture with simple spicule tracts
Abundant in reefs, mangroves and harbours

name: Poecilosclerida
description: Poecilosclerida are the most diverse demosponge order — encrusting and branching forms with signature microscleres, from red beard sponges to reef species.
keyCharacteristics: Largest demosponge order by species number
diagnosticFeatures: Ectosomal skeleton distinct from inner skeleton

name: Tetractinellida
description: Tetractinellida are stony demosponges with four-rayed spicules — massive barrel and ball sponges such as Geodia of cold deep waters.
keyCharacteristics: Massive globular or barrel growth forms
Cold and deep waters well represented

name: Tethyida
description: Tethyida are burrowing and ball sponges — orange golf-ball sponges such as Tethya with radiating spicule bundles.
keyCharacteristics: Spherical body with radiating spicule cortex
Burrowing species in sand as well as rock forms
diagnosticFeatures: Strongyloxeas radiating from a central core

name: Homosclerophorida
description: Homosclerophorida are encrusting homoscleromorph sponges — thin colourful sheets such as Oscarella on Mediterranean rocks.
keyCharacteristics: Thin encrusting sheets on shaded rock
Soft slimy texture without harsh spicules

name: Spongillidae
description: Spongillidae are the freshwater sponges — green encrusting colonies of lakes and rivers, including Spongilla.

name: Spongiidae
description: Spongiidae are commercial bath sponges — soft spongin skeletons of Spongia and Hippospongia harvested in the Mediterranean and Caribbean.
keyCharacteristics: Harvested, farmed and traded as bath sponges
diagnosticFeatures: No mineral spicules at any stage

name: Clionaidae
description: Clionaidae are boring sponges excavating limestone and shells — Cliona species recycle reef carbonate while filtering plankton.
keyCharacteristics: Papillae dotting rock surfaces above hidden tissue
Yellow, orange or green exposed colour

name: Sycettidae
description: Sycettidae are tubular calcareous sponges — the Sycon group with a fringed osculum crowning each tube.
keyCharacteristics: Clustered tubes with hairy fringed openings

name: Clathrinidae
description: Clathrinidae are network calcareous sponges — yellow cushions of fused tubes such as Clathrina on shaded rock.

name: Euplectellidae
description: Euplectellidae are lattice glass sponges — the Venus’ flower basket with its caged shrimp pair, trawled from deep Pacific slopes.
keyCharacteristics: Rigid lattice of fused six-rayed spicules
Lifelong shrimp symbionts inside the cage
diagnosticFeatures: Root tuft anchoring in soft sediment

name: Aphrocallistidae
description: Aphrocallistidae are reef-forming cloud sponges — giant white funnels building deep sponge reefs of the Pacific Northwest.
keyCharacteristics: Large funnel and tube growth on deep reefs
White to cream colouration in life
diagnosticFeatures: Loose hexactine skeleton stiffened by fused joints

name: Chalinidae
description: Chalinidae are branching tubular demosponges — Haliclona pipe sponges common on reefs, pilings and seagrass beds.

name: Microcionidae
description: Microcionidae are encrusting red-orange sponges — Clathria beard sponges coating rocks and shells in coastal waters.
diagnosticFeatures: Chelae microscleres in the surface layer

name: Geodiidae
description: Geodiidae are massive ball sponges — Geodia species forming stony spheres on cold-water reefs and slopes.
keyCharacteristics: Distinct pale cortex over darker interior

name: Tethyidae
description: Tethyidae are ball sponges — the orange golf-ball sponge Tethya with radiating spicule bundles and surface buds.
keyCharacteristics: Spherical body with warty budding surface

name: Oscarellidae
description: Oscarellidae are slimy encrusting sponges without harsh skeletons — Oscarella sheets in Mediterranean caves and shaded walls.
keyCharacteristics: Thin slimy sheets without mineral skeleton

name: Irciniidae
description: Irciniidae are leathery horny sponges — Ircinia species with tough fibre skeletons on Mediterranean reefs.
keyCharacteristics: Dark grey to brown massive forms

name: Spongilla
description: Spongilla are green freshwater sponges encrusting submerged wood and stone in lakes and slow rivers.
keyCharacteristics: Green encrusting sheets in sunlit shallows

name: Spongia
description: Spongia are fine bath sponges of the Mediterranean — soft harvested skeletons of the classic bath trade.
keyCharacteristics: Fine soft texture prized for bathing
Cup and fan growth on reefs
diagnosticFeatures: Dark living tissue over pale skeleton

name: Hippospongia
description: Hippospongia are honeycomb bath sponges with large open pores — Caribbean and Mediterranean harvested species.

name: Cliona
description: Cliona are boring sponges hollowing limestone, shells and coral — yellow papillae marking hidden excavating tissue.

name: Sycon
description: Sycon are tubular calcareous sponges — white clustered tubes with fringed openings on shaded marine rocks.
keyCharacteristics: Slender tubes crowned by hairy oscula
Clustered colonies on shells and rock

name: Clathrina
